title: US Makes Visa Bond Program Permanent for 50 Countries, Raises Cap to $20,000
excerpt: The State Department has converted its year-long visa bond pilot into a permanent policy, increasing the maximum bond from $15,000 to $20,000 for B-1/B-2 visa applicants from 50 countries with high overstay rates.
body:
• The U.S. State Department has made its visa bond program permanent for nationals of 50 countries, replacing the 12-month pilot that was set to expire on August 5, 2026.
  • The maximum bond amount has been raised from $15,000 to $20,000, with consular officers retaining discretion to set bonds at $5,000, $10,000, $15,000, or the new $20,000 tier.
  • The program, which targets B-1/B-2 business and tourist visa applicants from countries with high overstay rates, reported a 97% compliance rate during the pilot phase.
  • India is not on the current list, but neighboring Bangladesh and Nepal are among the 50 countries affected, and the policy signals a broader tightening of U.S. immigration controls.

From Pilot to Permanent

The Trump administration has converted its visa bond pilot program into a permanent fixture of U.S. immigration policy, the State Department announced this week. The move comes just days before the 12-month pilot was set to expire on August 5, 2026, and raises the maximum bond amount from $15,000 to $20,000.

https://x.com/CTVNews/status/2083266857042051486

Under the permanent program, nationals of 50 countries who apply for B-1 (business) or B-2 (tourist) visas will continue to be required to post refundable cash bonds as a condition of visa issuance. Consular officers will now have four bond tiers to choose from — $5,000, $10,000, $15,000, or the newly added $20,000 — based on their assessment of each applicant's likelihood of overstaying.

The pilot program, launched on August 20, 2025, under a Temporary Final Rule published in the Federal Register, was originally designed to test whether monetary bonds could reduce visa overstays and whether the State Department could operationally manage such a system. The administration has now concluded both answers are yes.

A Rapid Expansion

The program's growth over the past year has been dramatic. It began with just two countries — Malawi and Zambia — in August 2025. By October 2025, four more nations were added: The Gambia, Mauritania, Sao Tome and Principe, and Tanzania. A major expansion in January 2026 brought the total to 38 countries, and a further addition of 12 nations on April 2, 2026 pushed the count to 50.

The 50 countries span Africa, Asia, Latin America, and Oceania. The full list includes Algeria, Angola, Antigua and Barbuda, Bangladesh, Benin, Bhutan, Botswana, Burundi, Cabo Verde, Cambodia, Central African Republic, Cote d'Ivoire, Cuba, Djibouti, Dominica, Ethiopia, Fiji, Gabon, The Gambia, Georgia, Grenada, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Kyrgyzstan, Lesotho, Malawi, Mauritania, Mauritius, Mongolia, Mozambique, Namibia, Nepal, Nicaragua, Nigeria, Papua New Guinea, Sao Tome and Principe, Senegal, Seychelles, Tajikistan, Tanzania, Togo, Tonga, Tunisia, Turkmenistan, Tuvalu, Uganda, Vanuatu, Venezuela, Zambia, and Zimbabwe.

"The visa bond program has already proven effective at drastically reducing the number of visa recipients who overstay their visas and illegally remain in the United States."

— U.S. State Department

The Compliance Numbers

The State Department has pointed to the pilot's results as justification for making the program permanent. According to department figures, nearly 1,000 foreign nationals were issued visas under the bond requirement during the pilot phase, and 97% of bonded travelers returned home on time in compliance with their visa terms.

By contrast, the department noted that in the final year of the Biden administration, more than 44,000 visitors from the 50 countries now covered by the bond program overstayed their visas. The department has estimated the program saves U.S. taxpayers up to $800 million per year in removal costs, noting it costs over $18,000 on average to deport an individual who remains in the country illegally.

The bond applies only to B-1 and B-2 visa categories. Student visas (F-1), exchange visitor visas (J-1), work visas (H-1B), immigrant visas, and diplomatic visas are not affected. Visas issued under the program are valid for a single entry within three months, with stays generally capped at 30 days — far shorter than the standard six-month admission period for B-2 tourists.

How It Works

Applicants must pay the bond through the U.S. Treasury's Pay.gov platform after being directed to do so by a consular officer. They must also submit DHS Form I-352 (Immigration Bond form). The bond is returned in full if the traveler departs on time, never travels, or is denied admission at the port of entry.

Travelers who post bonds must enter and exit the U.S. exclusively through designated commercial airports. Land crossings, charter flights, general aviation, and seaports are not permitted — a requirement that some immigration attorneys have flagged as particularly restrictive.

Posting a bond does not guarantee visa issuance, and payments made without consular direction or through third-party websites are not refunded.

What This Means for the Indian Diaspora

India is not among the 50 countries currently subject to the visa bond requirement. However, neighboring Bangladesh and Nepal are on the list, directly affecting travel plans for nationals of those countries who have family or business ties across South Asia.

For the broader Indian diaspora, the program's permanence signals the continued tightening of U.S. immigration controls under the Trump administration, which has also implemented travel bans affecting 19 countries, aggressive deportation campaigns, and heightened scrutiny of visa applications including social media screening.

Immigration attorneys have warned that the bond requirement — while technically refundable — acts as a de facto financial barrier for applicants from lower-income countries who may not have $20,000 in liquid capital available upfront. The raised cap amplifies this concern.

What to Watch

With the program now permanent, the State Department retains the authority to add or remove countries from the list based on overstay rates, screening deficiencies, and other immigration risk factors. The department has historically provided at least 15 days' notice before adding new countries.

Whether the list expands further — and whether the program's scope eventually widens beyond B-1/B-2 visas — will be closely watched by immigration advocates, travel industry groups, and diaspora communities around the world. The U.S. Travel Association has previously raised concerns that the policy adds friction at a time when international travel to the United States is already declining, with visitation down 5.5% last year and travel from some markets dropping over 20%.
